idiom_name: RAII owner class (Rule of Five) - the destructor is the release point
implementation_notes: C++ replaces the Dispose protocol with the object's own lifetime: the destructor is invoked whenever the object's lifetime ends (end of scope, delete expression, thread or program termination), so the classic explicit 'call Dispose' step disappears and correctness is enforced by the type system - a non-copyable owner with move semantics that transfer responsibility. Resources held as members are released by their own destructors when the owner is destroyed, so the cascade is automatic and ordered (members destroyed in reverse construction order), and borrowed resources are simply references or raw pointers the owner never releases. Keep a classic explicit-release form only where release must be observable or interactive (a Close() that flushes and can fail, a resource returned to a pool) - then expose Close()/reset() alongside the destructor and make it idempotent.
pitfalls: Without a virtual destructor, deleting a derived object through a base pointer skips the derived release path; make the base destructor virtual (or protected and non-virtual).
A destructor must not let exceptions escape (implicitly noexcept since C++11): if the release step can fail, provide an explicit Close() and leave the destructor as the no-throw fallback.
Copying an owner duplicates the release obligation - delete the copy operations or implement the full Rule of Five so only one object owns the resource.

variants.name: Smart pointer with a custom deleter
variants.idiom_name: std::unique_ptr<T, Deleter> / std::shared_ptr as the ownership handle
variants.implementation_notes: Instead of a bespoke owner class, put the resource behind a standard smart pointer whose deleter is the release call: unique_ptr<FILE, decltype(&fclose)> closes on scope exit, and shared_ptr with a custom deleter (or a make_shared object plus a wrapper) extends the same discipline to shared ownership - the managed object is disposed of via the associated deleter when the pointer is destroyed or reset, and reset() is the explicit release. Choose this when ownership is single, when the resource is a C handle rather than a class, or when several owners must keep the resource alive; keep a named Close() when release is an operation with observable errors or pool semantics.
pitfalls: A shared_ptr deleter must not close a handle the object does not own; give borrowed handles a non-owning pointer or reference instead.

unique_ptr's default deleter uses delete, so unique_ptr<Base> on a Derived object still needs a virtual destructor - unique_ptr does not rescue that (shared_ptr captures the concrete deleter, so it differs).
A custom deleter that can throw makes the destructor path unsafe; mark it noexcept and report failures through an explicit reset-with-result or Close() call.
